objects.title: The Triangulum Galaxy
objects.subtitle: Messier 33, a spiral galaxy in Triangulum
objects.what: The third-largest galaxy in our small group of neighbours, after Andromeda and our own Milky Way: a loose spiral of some 40 billion stars. The blue knot at the left, NGC 604, is a cloud where new stars are being born, 1,500 light-years across. From this far away, one pixel of the picture is 10 light-years wide: more than twice the way from the Sun to the nearest star.
facts: 29,000 light-years; the whole galaxy is about twice that
2.7 million years ago, as the ice ages began
The disc is grey on purpose: these frames cannot measure its faint colour. White stars lean a little green
objects.made: 66 of 104 frames of 15 s; 34 were trailed by a tracking fault that was fixed during the run
objects.how: 16.5 minutes of light on one field, under a clear sky
specs: 104 taken, 66 kept. 34 frames were trailed by a tracking fault that was fixed during the run: the drive let go of both motors for about 5 s now and then, leaving each star a dot with a tail of 4 to 9 arcsec. 4 more had soft stars (4.4 to 4.7 arcsec). Clear: every untrailed frame within 5 percent of the run's star brightness

Shown only where the light can carry it, 0.4 percent of the picture: the stars, the core, the brightest star-forming clouds such as NGC 604. The disc is grey on purpose. objects.title: Almach
objects.subtitle: Gamma Andromedae, a gold and blue double star in Andromeda
objects.what: To the eye it is one star in Andromeda. A telescope splits it in two: a gold giant and a small blue companion, a favourite for the contrast of their colours. The blue one is really three stars, too close together for this picture to separate. Everything here, both stars and the dark between them, would fit in half a light-year.
facts: At least 1,000 times as far apart as the Earth is from the Sun: six days for light to cross
Around 1676, the year the speed of light was first measured
The colours are as the camera recorded them, with nothing added: the gold star is probably a little more orange than this, and the blue one a little bluer
objects.made: The sharpest 5 of 13 frames of 1/60 s
objects.how: The sharpest 5 of 13 frames, each a sixtieth of a second, at the sensor's own scale
specs: 5 x 1/60 s at ISO 400: a twelfth of a second of light. The primary did not clip: the brightest pixel of any colour plane in any frame is 72 percent of the 14-bit ceiling

13 taken, the sharpest 5 kept: the primary 3.03 to 3.46 arcsec wide (half-flux) in those, 3.65 to 4.31 in the 8 left out. A sixtieth of a second freezes the air, so a frame is sharp or it is not, and every frame added softens the star: all 13 give 3.70 arcsec against 3.32 for these 5

13 October 2026, after midnight, over 5 minutes. Nearly overhead

9.55 arcsec apart (standard error 0.09) at position angle 62.3 degrees (0.3): two-star fits to each of the 13 frames. With the model's own error, 9.6 plus or minus 0.15 arcsec at 62 plus or minus 1 degrees. The primary is 9.0 times the companion in the camera's green (2.4 magnitudes)
No darks and no flat. Each frame's sky median taken off per colour plane, one hot pixel repaired. The pair sits at the middle of the sensor, where a flat would change it by well under a percent

RAW colour planes (no demosaic). Shift only: each plane of each frame placed on its own centroid of the primary, at the true sensor position of every sample, as square drops of 1 px (drizzle). Each frame scaled to the run's median brightness first, since the star twinkles 8 percent from frame to frame
From a plate-solved 15 s frame of the same field, taken just before with the camera untouched: in a sixtieth of a second there are no other stars to solve on

The camera's daylight white balance (red x 2.67, blue x 1.24) and its own colour matrix, no star-colour calibration, saturation x 1.0. Red over green and blue over green: primary 1.09 and 0.56, companion 0.72 and 1.02. The companion is the bluer star in 13 of 13 frames; the primary's red halo spills onto it, so it is bluer than shown

Brightness smoothed 0.8 px, colour 1.5 px, arcsinh stretch. Black at the 60th percentile, white at the brightest channel of the brightest pixel, S-curve 0.15, no saturation added. Dark sky smoothed (bilateral, 2 px) and without colour
The companion is itself a close pair, about half an arcsecond apart: far inside the 3.3 arcsec blur of the air on this night. A seeing-limited picture; nothing finer than 2 to 3 arcsec is shown

objects.title: NGC 891
objects.subtitle: A spiral galaxy in Andromeda, seen edge on
objects.what: A spiral galaxy much like our own, seen almost exactly from the side. The dark line down its middle is dust in the disc, the same kind of dust that draws the dark lanes through our Milky Way on a clear night. This is roughly how our own galaxy would look from outside: a thin disc of stars with a warm bulge of older stars at its centre.
facts: 200,000 light-years; the disc shown is about 100,000 long, the size of our own galaxy
About 30 million years ago, when giant hornless rhinos, among the largest land mammals ever, walked Asia
Seven and a half minutes of light is too little for the faint tips of the disc: about a tenth of its length is missing at each end

objects.title: Messier 77
objects.subtitle: NGC 1068, a spiral galaxy in Cetus with an active centre
objects.what: A spiral galaxy seen nearly face on, and one of the nearest and brightest galaxies with an active centre. Deep in its middle, gas is falling toward a black hole of roughly ten million Suns and blazing as it falls, which helps make the centre shine like a star. Galaxies like this are called Seyfert galaxies, after Carl Seyfert, who described them in 1943.
facts: About 47 million light-years (not well known: estimates run from 33 to 62 million)
Roughly 200,000 light-years; the bright disc shown is roughly 35,000 across
Roughly 47 million years ago, when the ancestors of whales still walked on land
This picture shows the bright heart of the galaxy only. Its faint outer arms and ring, about three times as wide, are not seen

objects.title: NGC 1535
objects.subtitle: Cleopatra's Eye, a planetary nebula in Eridanus
objects.what: This is what a star like the Sun does at the end: it puffs its outer layers off into space, and the bare, hot core left behind makes them glow. The bright middle of the disc is that core, on its way to becoming a white dwarf; the faint shell round the disc is gas the star threw off earlier. William Herschel found it in 1785.
facts: Roughly 6,000 light-years (not well known: estimates run from 5,000 to 7,500)
16 light-years; the nebula with its faint shell is nearly 2 across, the bright disc about two thirds of one
Roughly 6,000 years ago, before the pyramids and probably before writing
The nebula glows in a blue-green from oxygen that is purer than any screen can show, so the screen's nearest colour stands in for it
objects.how: Two minutes of light, low in the sky: the softest picture of the night
specs: 30 x 4 s at ISO 1600: 120 seconds. Nothing clipped: the nebula peaks at 3 percent of the range in a 4 s frame

33 taken, 30 kept. One was taken while the mount was still re-centring after the telescope's computer was restarted mid-run; one had soft stars (6.55 arcsec against a limit of 6.5); one was trailed. The frames came in two runs either side of the restart, 17 and 13 kept, with the nebula in two different places on the sensor
0.777 arcsec per pixel: one pixel per 2 x 2 colour cell, never enlarged. Stars 5.8 arcsec wide (half-flux): the softest picture of the night, because it was the lowest
9.3 x 6.2 arcmin: a 720 x 480 crop round the nebula, turned by quarter turns only (no resampling after the stack). North 36 degrees clockwise of up
13 October 2026, after midnight, over 17 minutes. About 40 degrees up

Rotation and shift on 35 to 70 stars; the field turned 0.38 degrees. The air is a prism this low: red and blue star images sat 0.79 arcsec apart, measured on 22 stars and taken out in the one resampling (0.02 left). For the nebula's own light, which is not starlight, blue is still about 0.15 arcsec off

No darks and no flat frames were taken. Divided by the night's flat, built from the open sky of the NGC 891 run. This run's own sky is too faint in 4 s to check dust near the nebula; the odd and the even frames, each with frames of both runs, agree to 1 percent on the nebula. Hot pixels from the run itself (690 to 760 per colour plane)

RAW colour planes (no demosaic), hot pixels by 3 x 3 median, registered on stars with rotation, sigma-clipped weighted mean. One sky constant per colour per frame; in the picture only, a sky plane per colour, under 1.5 DN across it

The blue-green inner disc. The central star, as a star-wide bright core in the middle of it. The faint outer shell: in the ring 14 to 25 arcsec out the green light is 10.0 DN where the disc's own blur would leave 2.2, 73 times the noise, and the odd and the even frames each show it (55 and 65 times). The light ends 28 to 34 arcsec from the centre

Any structure inside the disc, or a sharp edge between disc and shell: with stars 5.8 arcsec wide the two run into each other. A small brighter spot in the shell about 17 arcsec out repeats in both halves and is not identified

The camera's daylight white balance and colour matrix, no saturation added. The nebula shines mostly in doubly ionised oxygen at 501 nm, a green-blue outside what a screen can show: the matrix gives it a negative red, which is shown as zero across the disc. That is the colour space, not the sensor

Brightness smoothed 1 px, colour 3.5 px, arcsinh stretch. Black at the 60th percentile, S-curve 0.15. Dark sky smoothed (median 3 px, bilateral 4 px) but kept below the shell on purpose: the shell's outer edge is grainy at full size, which is the stack's own noise

objects.title: The Crab Nebula
objects.subtitle: Messier 1, the wreck of an exploded star in Taurus
objects.what: What is left of a star that blew itself apart. Astronomers in China saw the explosion in 1054: a new star bright enough to see in daylight for three weeks. The cloud is still flying outward at about 1,500 km a second. At its centre is the collapsed core of the star, no bigger than a city, spinning about 30 times a second.
facts: 20 light-years; the nebula is about 13 long and 8 wide
Around 4500 BC, before writing was invented
The lumpy, lopsided shape is real: two separate halves of the frames show the same shape. The nebula's famous red threads are not seen, so it has one warm colour here

objects.title: Messier 78
objects.subtitle: A cloud of dust in Orion, lit by the stars inside it
objects.what: This cloud does not shine by itself. It is dust, lit by the young stars inside it the way fog glows round a street lamp, and it is bluer than its stars for the same reason the daytime sky is blue. The black band above it is more of the same dust, unlit. It is one of the brightest clouds of its kind in the sky, and part of the great cloud where Orion's stars are being born.
facts: Nearly 7 light-years; the glow shown is about 2 across
Around the year 680, when the Maya were building their great cities
The cloud measures bluer than the stars that light it, but that is only a cool white beside them, and no colour was added to make it blue. Its faint outer parts are not shown

Each of these repeats in the odd and the even halves of the frames. The glow round the two stars, 20 times the scatter of blank sky. objects.title: Hubble's Variable Nebula
objects.subtitle: NGC 2261, a fan of dust lit by the star R Monocerotis
objects.what: A fan of dust lit from its tip by a young star, like a torch beam in fog. It changes: clouds of dust close to the star cast shadows that sweep up the fan over weeks and months, so no two pictures of it taken a season apart are the same. Edwin Hubble studied it for years, and in January 1949 he made it the first thing photographed with the 200 inch telescope on Palomar.
facts: 7.5 light-years; the fan shown is about one light-year long
Around 470 BC, about when Socrates was born

objects.title: NGC 2392
objects.subtitle: A planetary nebula in Gemini
objects.what: The same kind of object as tonight's NGC 1535, taken the same way. The star at the centre was once much like the Sun. It has thrown off its outer layers twice: the faint outer disc first, and the bright inner shell after it. What is left of the star is the hot point in the middle, which makes both of them glow. William Herschel found it in 1787.
facts: Roughly 6,500 light-years (not well known: estimates run from 3,000 to 7,000)
About 18 light-years; the outer disc is about 2 across, the inner shell a little over half of one
Roughly 6,500 years ago: if that distance is right, before writing was invented
Cloud was thickening as this was taken, so it holds little more than a minute of light. And as with NGC 1535, the nebula's blue-green is purer than any screen can show
objects.made: 21 of 32 frames of 4 s; cloud took the last ten
objects.how: 84 seconds of light, taken the same way as NGC 1535; cloud took the last ten frames
specs: 21 x 4 s at ISO 1600: 84 seconds. Nothing clipped: the nebula peaks at 8 percent of the range in a 4 s frame

32 taken, 21 kept. The first after the slew was dropped by rule; the last ten were lost to cloud, when the stars fell below half their brightness. None trailed. Cloud thickened through the run, so the later frames kept are scaled up and weighted down: the stack is worth about 15 clear frames, a minute of light
0.777 arcsec per pixel: one pixel per 2 x 2 colour cell, never enlarged, as for NGC 1535. Stars 5.0 arcsec wide (half-flux)
9.3 x 6.2 arcmin: a 720 x 480 crop round the nebula, turned by quarter turns only (no resampling after the stack). North 38 degrees clockwise of up

No darks and no flat frames were taken. Divided by the night's flat, built from the open sky of the NGC 891 run. This run's own sky is too faint in 4 s to check the flat's dust, and the nebula sat on the same pixels throughout, so a shadow there would not average out. Hot pixels from the run itself (580 to 620 per colour plane)

RAW colour planes (no demosaic), hot pixels by 3 x 3 median, registered on stars with rotation, sigma-clipped weighted mean. One sky constant per colour per frame; in the picture only, a sky plane per colour is subtracted as well

The central star, a clear star-like point, far stronger than in NGC 1535: 716 DN at the centre against 136 at 4.7 arcsec out. The inner shell, a blue-green shoulder of light from about 4 to 10 arcsec out. The fainter outer disc: in the ring 14 to 25 arcsec out the green light is 17.3 DN where spilled inner light would leave 0.9, 136 times the noise, and the odd and the even frames each show it (95 and 112 times). The light ends 28 to 34 arcsec from the centre

A dark gap between the star and the inner shell, the shell's rim as a ring, knots or filaments: with stars 5.0 arcsec wide the star's own image reaches the shell. The star images in this stack are slightly lopsided, so no claim is made about the nebula's shape

The camera's daylight white balance and colour matrix, no saturation added. As with NGC 1535, the green-blue of doubly ionised oxygen at 501 nm lies outside what a screen can show: the matrix gives it a negative red, shown as zero across the outer disc. The stars read slightly green-yellow, as in tonight's other pictures: that is the camera, not the stars

Brightness smoothed 1.5 px (NGC 1535: 1.0), colour 3.5 px, arcsinh stretch. Black at the 60th percentile, S-curve 0.15. Dark sky smoothed (median 3 px, bilateral 4 px). The 8th magnitude star north of the nebula is five times brighter than the nebula's centre: its core is at full scale in green for a few pixels

objects.title: NGC 2419
objects.subtitle: A globular cluster in Lynx, at the far edge of our galaxy
objects.what: A ball of hundreds of thousands of ancient stars, nearly twice as far away as the Large Magellanic Cloud, the Milky Way's big companion galaxy. It is so far out that it was once thought to be adrift between galaxies, and was called the Intergalactic Wanderer; in fact it orbits the Milky Way. The two bright stars beside it are in our own neighbourhood, hundreds or thousands of times nearer.
facts: About 1,400 light-years; the haze shown is about 200 across, and one pixel is more than a light-year
About 300,000 years ago, around when our own species first appears in the fossil record
A short picture, partly through cloud: only the bright middle of the cluster shows, less than half its full width. Its speckle is real, but no single star can be picked out
objects.made: 17 of 29 frames of 15 s; cloud took the other twelve
objects.how: 4.25 minutes of light, between patches of cloud
specs: 29 taken, 17 kept. All 12 dropped were lost to cloud: the run began and ended under thin cloud in patches, the stars dimmer under a brighter sky, with 13 clear frames in a row in the middle. Four thin frames, at 80 to 90 percent, are used, scaled up and weighted down
